detailHeading: Why fences lean in Georgian Bay country
detailBody: Most leaning fences start at the posts. Each winter, wet soil around Collingwood freezes and expands, which lifts posts that were set too shallow. After a few freeze-thaw cycles, the post tilts and the panels pull with it.

Rot is the other common cause. Posts sit in damp soil for years, and the wood breaks down at grade, where you cannot see it. A post that wobbles when you push it is usually rotted at the base, even if the top looks fine.

Fixing a few posts and boards often adds years to a fence that is otherwise sound. If most posts are soft or the boards are failing along the whole run, Keith will tell you when replacing a section makes more sense than patching it.

faqs.q: Can you match my existing fence boards?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Keith matches the board width, profile and spacing with new lumber. New wood looks lighter at first, so staining or sealing the repair helps it blend with the older sections over time.

faqs.q: Should I repair or replace my fence?
faqs.a: If the posts are mostly solid and the damage is limited to a few boards, a gate or one section, repair is usually the practical choice. If many posts are rotted, replacing the run can make more sense. Keith gives you an honest view in the estimate.

faqs.q: How do you stop new posts from rotting?
faqs.a: Keith uses pressure-treated posts rated for ground contact, sets them in concrete shaped to shed water, and keeps the top of the footing above grade. These steps help keep the post dry where rot usually starts.

faqs.q: Can you fix a gate that drags or won’t latch?
faqs.a: Yes. Sagging gates are a common repair. Keith checks the hinge post first, then squares the frame, adds bracing if needed, and replaces worn hinges or latches so the gate closes properly.

faqs.q: Do you repair fences at cottages?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith works on fences at homes and cottages across the area. Let him know how to access the property and whether you will be there, and he will plan the repair around that.

detailHeading: Why drywall patches show, and how to avoid it
detailBody: Most patches show for three reasons. The compound goes on too thick, the edges are not feathered wide enough, or the repair is painted without primer. Bare compound takes paint differently from the wall around it, so the patch shows as a dull or shiny spot.
Keith builds repairs in thin coats, sands each one and primes before paint. On textured walls and ceilings, he matches the texture first so the patch reads the same under side light from a window.

Water stains need more care. In Collingwood homes and lakeside cottages, ceiling stains often come from ice dams, roof leaks or a slow drip under a bathroom. The source has to be fixed first. If the drywall stays soft or shows mould, Keith replaces that section instead of painting over it.

faqs.q: Can you match my existing wall texture?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. Keith matches common textures like orange peel and knockdown, and feathers and sands smooth finishes. He checks the result under side light before priming, since that is where a poor match shows.

faqs.q: Do you paint after the drywall repair?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith primes every repair and can paint the patched wall or ceiling. Painting the full wall, corner to corner, usually gives the most even result, especially if the existing paint is older.

faqs.q: What if there is mould behind water-damaged drywall?
faqs.a: Keith removes the damaged section so you can see the cavity. Small areas of surface mould on framing are cleaned and dried. If the mould is widespread, he will tell you and recommend a remediation specialist before any new drywall goes up.

faqs.q: Should I fix the leak before calling about drywall?
faqs.a: Yes, the leak needs to stop first. If you are not sure where the water came from, Keith can look while assessing the damage. Where the source needs a licensed plumber or a roofer, that is identified in the estimate and coordinated.

faqs.q: Can you repair drywall in a rental or before a sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith patches holes and wear between tenants and before a listing, and can handle the touch-up painting so the rooms are clean and ready to show.

detailBody: A single repair rarely needs a general contractor. A kitchen, bathroom or basement project usually does, because the work involves several trades in a set order. Plumbing and electrical rough-in come before insulation and drywall. Drywall comes before tile, trim and paint. When that order slips, finished work gets torn out.

Keith plans that sequence up front and keeps the project on track. He does much of the carpentry and finishing himself and brings in licensed trades for the work they are required to do, such as electrical and gas.

For cottages around Georgian Bay, coordination matters even more. Owners are often away, so Keith keeps you updated and makes sure the right people are on site at the right stage. Work that needs a licensed trade is identified in the estimate before anything starts.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a handyman and a general contractor?
faqs.a: A handyman takes on individual repairs and smaller jobs. A general contractor manages a whole project, including the order of work and the trades involved. Keith does both, so a small job stays simple and a larger renovation has one person in charge.

detailHeading: Choosing flooring for Georgian Bay homes and cottages
detailBody: Humidity around Georgian Bay swings widely from summer to winter. Solid wood moves the most with those changes, which is why engineered hardwood and vinyl plank are popular here. Both handle seasonal swings better. If your cottage sits unheated in winter, check the product’s temperature rating before you buy.

For entries, kitchens, basements and cottage living areas, vinyl plank is a practical pick. It resists water and handles sand and grit well. Laminate suits bedrooms and living rooms but should stay out of areas that get wet.

A floor is only as good as what is under it. Keith checks the subfloor for squeaks, soft spots and dips before installing, fixes them first, and lets new flooring acclimate where the product calls for it.

faqs.q: What flooring works best for a cottage?
faqs.a: Vinyl plank is a common choice for cottages because it resists water and handles sand and grit. If the cottage is unheated in winter, check that the product is rated for those temperatures. Keith can talk through options before you buy.

faqs.q: Can you install flooring I have already bought?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith installs flooring you supply. Have the boxes on site and let him know the product, so he can check the installation requirements and plan the underlay, trim and transitions.

faqs.q: Can new flooring go over my existing floor?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Vinyl plank and laminate can go over some flat, solid floors, but not over carpet or soft, uneven surfaces. Floor height at doors and appliances also matters. Keith checks the existing floor and recommends removal where needed.

faqs.q: Do I need to move my furniture first?
faqs.a: It helps to clear small items, electronics and anything fragile. Talk to Keith about larger furniture when you review your estimate, so the plan covers who moves what and where it goes.

faqs.q: Why is subfloor preparation so important?
faqs.a: Most flooring problems start below the floor. Dips cause click joints to separate, high spots cause rocking, and loose panels cause squeaks. Fixing the subfloor first is what keeps a new floor flat and quiet.

Grouping repairs into one list makes sense. Keith can work through several items in one visit, and you get one estimate that covers the lot. Keep a running note on your phone of anything that sticks, squeaks, drips or rattles.

Some fixes point to a bigger issue. A door that keeps binding can mean settling, and a stain near a window can mean a failed seal. Keith will tell you what he sees and what he recommends, so you can decide what to do next.

detailBody: Kitchen cabinets get more handling than any wall in your house. Grease from cooking, hand oils and cleaning sprays all work against paint. A finish that looks good on day one can chip at the edges if the prep is rushed.

Keith removes doors and drawer fronts, labels each one, and degreases every surface before sanding. A bonding primer goes on next, followed by cabinet-grade paint in thin coats. Doors go back up only after the paint has cured enough to handle use.

Most solid wood and MDF cabinets paint well. Oak grain shows through paint unless it is filled first, so let Keith know if you want a smooth look. Thermofoil and laminate doors that are peeling need a different approach, and Keith will tell you if replacement is the better option.

faqs.q: Will painted cabinets hold up to daily use?
faqs.a: Yes, with proper prep and the right products. Degreasing, sanding and a bonding primer give the paint something to grip. Cabinet-grade paint cures to a hard finish that stands up to cleaning and regular handling.

faqs.q: Can all cabinets be painted?
faqs.a: Most wood and MDF cabinets paint well. Laminate and thermofoil can be painted in some cases with special primers, but peeling thermofoil is not a good candidate. Keith looks at your cabinets and tells you what will work.

faqs.q: Will the wood grain show through the paint?
faqs.a: Open-grain woods like oak show texture through paint. If you want a smooth, modern finish, the grain can be filled before priming. Let Keith know the look you want when you review your estimate.

faqs.q: Can I use my kitchen while the cabinets are painted?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The cabinet boxes are painted in place and the doors are painted away from the kitchen. Plan to empty the cabinets being painted and keep counters clear while the work is underway.

faqs.q: Should I replace my hardware at the same time?
faqs.a: It is a good time to do it. New handles and knobs finish the look, and Keith can fill old holes if the new hardware uses a different spacing. Bring your hardware choice to the estimate if you have one.

detailHeading: When a fixture swap needs a licensed plumber
detailBody: A fixture swap connects a new faucet, toilet or sink to supply and drain lines already in the same spot. That is the work Keith does. He shuts off the water, removes the old fixture, installs the new one with fresh supply lines and seals, and tests every joint.

Moving a sink, adding a fixture where there was none, or running new supply or drain lines is different. That work needs a licensed plumber. Keith identifies it in the estimate and coordinates it with one.

Older homes and cottages around Collingwood often have seized shut-off valves, corroded supply lines or mismatched fittings. Keith checks these before he starts, so you know if a valve or line needs replacing along with the fixture. If a cottage was closed for winter, mention it, since lines and fixtures may need a check after a freeze.

faqs.q: Can you install fixtures I already bought?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith installs faucets, toilets and sinks you supply. Have them on site and check the box for the parts list. Some fixtures need a specific supply line or adapter, and Keith can confirm that when you review the estimate.

faqs.q: Do I need a plumber to replace a faucet or toilet?
faqs.a: A straight swap on existing supply and drain lines is a common handyman job. New supply or drain runs, moved fixtures and larger plumbing changes need a licensed plumber. Keith identifies that work in the estimate and coordinates it.

faqs.q: What if my shut-off valve won’t close?
faqs.a: Old valves often seize or drip once they are turned. Keith can replace a faulty shut-off valve as part of the fixture swap, so you have reliable water control at that fixture from then on.

faqs.q: Can you work with older cottage plumbing?
faqs.a: Yes, within the scope of a fixture swap. Keith checks the condition of the valves, supply lines and drain connections first. If the older plumbing needs more than a swap, he will tell you and arrange a licensed plumber.

faqs.q: Can you help me choose a fixture?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith can tell you what will fit your existing sink, counter and connections, such as the faucet hole count or toilet rough-in size, so the fixture you buy suits the space.

detailHeading: Pressure washing after a Georgian Bay winter
detailBody: Winters around Collingwood leave road salt on driveways and garage floors, and damp shade near Georgian Bay feeds moss, mildew and green algae on siding, decks and north-facing walls. Left in place, algae keeps surfaces slippery and holds moisture against wood.

More pressure is not always better. High pressure can etch soft wood, scar composite, strip joint sand from interlock and push water behind siding. Keith matches the pressure, nozzle and cleaner to each surface, and uses a soft wash on siding.

Spring and early summer are popular times to wash, once the risk of frost has passed. If you plan to stain a deck or fence, wash it first and let the wood dry fully before staining. Keith can clean the surface and handle the stain or sealer as one job.

faqs.q: Is pressure washing safe for all surfaces?
faqs.a: Not at full pressure. Soft wood, composite, older mortar and siding all need gentler methods. Keith adjusts pressure and nozzles for each surface and uses a low-pressure soft wash on siding to avoid damage and water getting behind the panels.

faqs.q: When is the best time to pressure wash?
faqs.a: Spring and early summer work well around Collingwood, after the last frost, once salt and winter grime have built up. Washing in fall before closing a cottage also helps keep mildew from setting in over winter.

faqs.q: Do you use cleaning solutions?
faqs.a: For mildew, algae and heavy staining, Keith pre-treats the surface with a cleaner suited to the material. He wets down plants and protects landscaping near the work area. Plain water is enough for many jobs.

faqs.q: Should I pressure wash before staining my deck?
faqs.a: Yes. Stain needs a clean, dry surface to soak in and bond. Washing removes dirt, mildew and loose grey fibres. Let the wood dry fully before staining. Keith can do both the washing and the staining.

faqs.q: How often should I have my property washed?
faqs.a: Many homes and cottages need it once a year, often in spring. Shaded areas near trees or water can need it more often. Keith can tell you which surfaces need regular attention.

detailHeading: A maintenance rhythm for Collingwood homes and cottages
detailBody: Freeze-thaw cycles, heavy snow and lake humidity are hard on buildings around Georgian Bay. Caulking cracks, gutters fill with leaves and needles, and exterior wood takes on moisture. Many expensive repairs start as small issues no one had time to catch.

Spring and fall are the two key visits. In spring, check for winter damage, clear gutters and look at decks, railings and caulking. In fall, clear gutters again after the leaves drop, change furnace filters and seal gaps before the cold sets in.

For cottages and seasonal homes, regular visits matter more because no one is there to notice a problem. Keith works from a set task list, notes anything that needs repair, and checks with you before doing work beyond the plan.

faqs.q: What is included in a seasonal maintenance visit?
faqs.a: That depends on your property. A typical visit covers gutters, caulking, weatherstripping, filters, alarm batteries and a walk-around for damage. Keith builds the task list with you and notes any repairs he finds for your approval.

faqs.q: How often should I schedule maintenance?
faqs.a: Most homes do well with a spring and fall visit. Cottages, rentals and properties with more upkeep may need visits more often. Keith can suggest a schedule based on the property and how it is used.

faqs.q: Do you maintain cottages and seasonal homes?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith maintains homes and cottages across the area and can combine regular upkeep with cottage opening and closing. Let him know about access and anything you want checked while you are away.

faqs.q: Do you work with landlords and property managers?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith handles routine upkeep and small repairs for rental properties. For several units or ongoing work, see the property manager maintenance page or tell him about your properties when you request an estimate.

faqs.q: What if you find something that needs a licensed trade?
faqs.a: Keith notes it and lets you know. Work that needs a licensed electrician, plumber or gas technician is identified in the estimate and coordinated with a licensed trade before any of it goes ahead.
